title: Judges 12:1–7
context: The men of Ephraim confront Jephthah, angry that they were not called to fight Ammon, and threaten to burn his house. Jephthah answers that he called them and they did not come. The quarrel turns into civil war. The Gileadites seize the fords of the Jordan and test fleeing Ephraimites by asking them to say Shibboleth; those who say Sibboleth are killed. The number of the fallen is large, and interpreters discuss how such numbers in Judges should be understood. Jephthah judges six years and dies. Gideon had calmed a similar complaint from Ephraim with gentle words (8:1–3), and the contrast is instructive. Both traditions see here the tragedy of pride, harsh words, and tribal strife among God’s own people.

verses.text: The men of Ephraim were gathered together, and passed northward; and they said to Jephthah, “Why did you pass over to fight against the children of Ammon, and didn’t call us to go with you? We will burn your house around you with fire!”
verses.arminianNotes:
The men of Ephraim gather and confront Jephthah, angry that they were not called to fight Ammon, and threaten to burn his house. Their pride is wounded.

Arminian readers note that Ephraim’s anger is their own choice, and their threat escalates a dispute that could have been resolved.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Ephraim had made a similar complaint to Gideon (8:1–3). Tribal pride is a recurring problem in Judges.

Both traditions see in Ephraim’s anger the danger of pride and jealousy among God’s people.

verses.text: Jephthah said to them, “I and my people were at great strife with the children of Ammon; and when I called you, you didn’t save me out of their hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah says he called Ephraim during the struggle with Ammon, but they did not save him. He defends himself.

Arminian readers note that Jephthah’s account may be true, but his response lacks the gentleness that might have calmed the situation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the earlier narrative does not record Jephthah calling Ephraim, so interpreters differ on how to assess his claim.

Both traditions see in the exchange a breakdown of trust between tribes that should have been united.

verses.text: When I saw that you didn’t save me, I put my life in my hand, and passed over against the children of Ammon, and the LORD delivered them into my hand. Why then have you come up to me today, to fight against me?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah says he risked his life, crossed against Ammon, and the LORD delivered them, so why have they come to fight? He credits God and questions Ephraim.

Arminian readers note that Jephthah acknowledges God’s role, but his tone is confrontational.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Gideon answered a similar complaint with a soft answer (compare Proverbs 15:1), while Jephthah responds sharply.

Both traditions draw from the contrast a lesson about how words can calm or inflame conflict.

verses.text: Then Jephthah gathered together all the men of Gilead, and fought with Ephraim. The men of Gilead struck Ephraim, because they said, “You are fugitives of Ephraim, you Gileadites, in the middle of Ephraim, and in the middle of Manasseh.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah gathers the men of Gilead and fights Ephraim, after the Ephraimites insult the Gileadites as fugitives of Ephraim. Words lead to war.

Arminian readers note that the insult and the response are both choices that escalate into bloodshed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that civil war among God’s people is a sign of the moral decline that Judges traces.

Both traditions see here the tragedy of tribal strife, where insults and pride lead to the shedding of brothers’ blood.

verses.text: The Gileadites took the fords of the Jordan against the Ephraimites. Whenever a fugitive of Ephraim said, “Let me go over,” the men of Gilead said to him, “Are you an Ephraimite?” If he said, “No;”
verses.arminianNotes:
The Gileadites seize the fords of the Jordan, and when fleeing Ephraimites ask to cross, they ask whether they are Ephraimites. The trap is set.

Arminian readers note the cruelty of turning a place of passage into a place of death.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the fords, once a place where God brought Israel across in triumph (Joshua 3), become a place of division.

Both traditions read the scene as a sorrowful picture of brothers turned against one another.

verses.text: then they said to him, “Now say ‘Shibboleth;’ ” and he said “Sibboleth”; for he couldn’t manage to pronounce it correctly, then they seized him and killed him at the fords of the Jordan. At that time, forty-two thousand of Ephraim fell.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Gileadites tell them to say Shibboleth, and when they say Sibboleth, they are killed; forty-two thousand Ephraimites fall. A difference in pronunciation becomes a matter of life and death.

Arminian readers note the tragedy of identity being used to kill.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that interpreters discuss how large numbers in Judges should be understood. The scale shows the depth of the conflict.

Both traditions see here a warning against division that turns small differences into grounds for hatred among God’s people.

verses.text: Jephthah judged Israel six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died, and was buried in the cities of Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah judges Israel six years, dies, and is buried in the cities of Gilead. His story ends.

Arminian readers note that Jephthah’s life combined real faith with tragic choices, and his legacy is mixed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the burial notice is brief, and the phrase about the cities of Gilead is unusual; interpreters differ on its meaning.

Both traditions read Jephthah’s life soberly, recognizing that God used him while not approving every act (compare Hebrews 11:32).
